title: Enterprise Risk Management for Life Insurance Companies

blocks.h: On completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

items.h: Explain the purpose and scope of Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) in the context of a life insurance company and describe the principal international ERM frameworks — ISO 31000, COSO, and the IAIS Insurance Core Principles — and how they are applied in the Nigerian regulatory context.

Identify and describe the eight principal categories of risk faced by Nigerian life insurers — insurance risk, market risk, credit risk, operational risk, liquidity risk, regulatory risk, reputational risk, and cyber risk — and explain the specific drivers of each in the Nigerian operating environment.

Define risk appetite and risk tolerance, explain how Boards of Directors set and monitor risk limits, and describe the components of a Board-approved risk appetite statement for a life insurance company.
Describe the structure and purpose of the risk register and explain how Key Risk Indicators (KRIs) are selected, monitored, and reported as part of the ongoing risk management cycle.
Explain the Own Risk and Solvency Assessment (ORSA), describe its mandatory requirements under NIIRA 2025, and outline the process for conducting and reporting the ORSA to the Board and NAICOM.

Describe the three-lines-of-defence model as applied to life insurance risk governance, explain the roles of the Chief Risk Officer and the Board Risk Committee, and identify the governance failures that commonly undermine effective ERM in practice.

Assess the principal catastrophe risks facing Nigerian life insurers — pandemic, flood, and civil unrest — describe their potential impact on life insurance portfolios, and explain how each is managed within the ERM framework.

Describe NIIRA 2025’s mandatory risk management framework requirements, including the risk management policy obligations, the ORSA reporting timeline, and NAICOM’s supervisory intervention powers in response to identified risk management deficiencies.

Explain the components of a Business Continuity Management (BCM) framework for a life insurance company, including the Business Impact Analysis, recovery strategies, and the testing and maintenance cycle.

Describe the nature of climate risk as it applies to Nigerian life insurers, distinguishing between physical and transition risk dimensions, and explain how climate risk is incorporated into the insurer’s ERM framework and investment strategy.

blocks.text: 15.1 Introduction: Why Enterprise Risk Management Matters for Life Insurers

blocks.h: A life insurance company is, by its fundamental nature, a risk-taking enterprise. It accepts mortality, longevity, morbidity, and financial risks from policyholders and pensions beneficiaries and promises to pay defined benefits at uncertain future points. Every day it is in business, it is exposed to the possibility that actual experience — the rate at which people die, the returns earned on invested premiums, the costs of running the operation — will diverge adversely from the assumptions on which its products were priced and its reserves calculated.

Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) is the systematic, organisation-wide process by which a life insurer identifies all the risks it faces, assesses their likelihood and potential impact, decides how much of each risk it is willing to bear, and takes action to manage risks that exceed its tolerance. ERM is not a compliance exercise — it is a strategic function. An insurer that manages its risks well can price more accurately, hold less excess capital, respond faster to market opportunities, and sustain its solvency through adverse periods. An insurer that manages its risks poorly faces the prospect of unexpected losses, regulatory intervention, and ultimately insolvency.

The Nigerian life insurance market presents a distinctive risk landscape. Macroeconomic volatility — currency depreciation, high and volatile interest rates, inflation — creates asset-liability mismatches that demand active management. Security conditions in parts of the country create catastrophe mortality concentrations that pure individual underwriting cannot fully capture. Regulatory transformation under NIIRA 2025, including Risk-Based Capital, the ORSA requirement, and expanded NAICOM supervisory powers, has elevated the technical and governance demands on the risk function to a level comparable with international best practice. And the cyber and data risk environment is evolving faster than most Nigerian insurers’ technology and governance frameworks are adapting.

This chapter provides insurance professionals with a comprehensive understanding of the ERM framework, risk taxonomy, governance architecture, regulatory requirements, and specific risk categories that define the risk environment for a Nigerian life insurer in the NIIRA 2025 era.

ISO 31000:2018 (Risk Management — Guidelines) is the international standard published by the International Organization for Standardization that provides principles, a framework, and a process for managing risk across any type of organisation. It is the most widely referenced risk management standard globally and underpins the risk management language and process architecture used in most Nigerian regulated industries, including insurance.

The ISO 31000 framework rests on three foundational components: principles (the characteristics of effective risk management: integrated, structured, customised, inclusive, dynamic, informed, and continuously improving); a framework (the organisational architecture for embedding risk management: mandate and commitment, design, implementation, evaluation, and improvement); and a process (the operational cycle: communication and consultation, establishing context, risk assessment — identification, analysis, and evaluation — risk treatment, monitoring and review, and recording and reporting).

For a Nigerian life insurer, ISO 31000 provides the vocabulary and process architecture on which the company’s ERM policy and risk management manual are built. It is not prescriptive about specific risk categories or thresholds — it provides the container, not the content. The content is filled by the insurer’s own risk identification work and by the NAICOM regulatory requirements imposed by NIIRA 2025.

The Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission (COSO) published its updated Enterprise Risk Management — Integrating with Strategy and Performance framework in 2017. COSO ERM is more prescriptive than ISO 31000 and more explicitly integrated with corporate strategy: it frames ERM as a function that should inform and shape the company’s strategic objectives, not merely identify risks to those objectives after the fact.

The COSO 2017 framework is organised into five components and twenty principles, grouped into: governance and culture; strategy and objective-setting; performance; review and revision; and information, communication, and reporting. For a Nigerian life insurer, the most practically relevant COSO contributions are its explicit linkage of risk appetite to strategic planning, and its emphasis on embedding risk considerations into the performance management of all business functions — not just the risk function.

The International Association of Insurance Supervisors (IAIS) publishes Insurance Core Principles (ICPs) — the global standards for insurance regulation and supervision. ICP 8 (Risk Management and Internal Controls) is the specific standard governing the ERM obligations of insurers and sets expectations for: the risk management system; the internal control system; the internal audit function; and the actuarial function. NAICOM’s risk management requirements under NIIRA 2025 are substantially aligned with ICP 8, making an understanding of the ICP framework directly relevant to Nigerian life insurance practice.

ICP 16 (Enterprise Risk Management for Solvency Purposes) specifically requires insurers to have an ERM framework that is: comprehensive (covering all material risks); forward-looking (including stress testing and scenario analysis); integrated with the capital management process; and subject to Board oversight. ICP 16 is the foundation for the ORSA requirement (Section 15.6) and for the RBC framework introduced by NIIRA 2025.

rows: Process and principles: provides the universal language and cycle of risk management.
Basis for the company’s ERM policy manual, risk management process, and risk culture training.
Strategy integration: links risk management to strategic planning and performance.
Basis for Board-level risk appetite setting and integration of risk into business planning.
Regulatory standards: defines supervisory expectations for risk management in insurance.
Basis for NAICOM’s risk management requirements in NIIRA 2025 and the ORSA obligation.

blocks.text: 15.3 Categories of Risk in Nigerian Life Insurance

blocks.h: A comprehensive ERM framework requires the explicit identification and categorisation of every material risk the insurer faces. The standard risk taxonomy for a Nigerian life insurance company comprises eight categories:

Insurance risk is the risk that the actual experience of the insurer’s life portfolio will differ adversely from the assumptions made in pricing and reserving. It is the most fundamental risk category for a life insurer and the primary driver of the C1 capital charge under the NIIRA 2025 RBC framework.
Insurance risk in a Nigerian life insurer has four principal sub-components:

items.h: Mortality risk: The risk that more policyholders die than the pricing mortality assumption expected. Drivers in Nigeria include: high burden of communicable diseases (malaria, tuberculosis, HIV/AIDS); limited access to healthcare in rural and peri-urban populations; road traffic accident mortality among insured working-age individuals; and the impact of climate-related health events on population mortality.

Longevity risk: The risk that annuitants and pension beneficiaries live longer than expected, requiring the insurer to pay benefits for longer than priced. Longevity risk is the mirror image of mortality risk and is the primary concern for annuity and retirement product lines.

Morbidity risk: The risk that Critical Illness and Total and Permanent Disability claims exceed expected rates. Driven by rising prevalence of non-communicable diseases (hypertension, diabetes, cancer) among the insured population.

Lapse and persistency risk: The risk that policyholders lapse policies at rates different from those assumed in pricing, adversely affecting profitability. Mass lapse scenarios — where economic shock drives a simultaneous wave of surrenders — represent a particularly severe stress scenario for savings product portfolios.

blocks.h: Market risk is the risk of loss arising from adverse movements in financial market prices: interest rates, equity prices, real estate values, exchange rates, and inflation. For a Nigerian life insurer, the most significant market risk sub-components are:

items.h: Interest rate risk: Life insurance liabilities are long-duration: a 20-year endowment creates a liability that extends two decades. If the insurer’s investment assets are shorter-duration than its liabilities, a fall in interest rates will reduce investment income while the discounted value of long-term liabilities rises — an asset-liability mismatch that destroys the surplus. Nigeria’s history of extreme interest rate volatility (from 22% in 2024 to single digits in some prior periods) makes this a material risk.

Currency risk: Nigerian life insurers that denominate policies in Naira but invest in foreign assets, or that have international reinsurance recoveries denominated in foreign currency, face currency translation risk. Naira devaluation reduces the Naira value of foreign-currency assets and inflates the Naira cost of foreign-currency liabilities.

Equity and property risk: Insurers holding equities and real estate in their investment portfolios are exposed to capital value fluctuations. The Nigerian equities market (NGX) and commercial property market have both experienced significant volatility, creating mark-to-market risk in investment portfolios.

Inflation risk: Persistent above-target inflation increases the real cost of claims (particularly for expense-sensitive products), erodes the real value of fixed-income investments, and may trigger policyholder demands for benefit inflation protection that was not priced into the original product.

blocks.h: Credit risk is the risk of financial loss arising from the default or credit quality deterioration of a counterparty. For a Nigerian life insurer, the primary credit risk exposures are:

items.h: Bond and fixed income investment defaults: Corporate bonds and sub-sovereign bonds held in the investment portfolio carry default risk. FGN bonds (Federal Government of Nigeria bonds) carry sovereign risk, which, while low by Nigerian standards, is not zero given Nigeria’s history of debt restructuring discussions.

Reinsurance counterparty risk: The insurer holds a reinsurance asset representing the amount recoverable from reinsurers on outstanding claims and future policy obligations. If a reinsurer defaults, the cedant insurer remains liable to policyholders for the full benefit — the reinsurance recovery disappears but the liability remains. Under IFRS 17, this credit risk must be quantified and provisioned for as an expected credit loss.

Premium debtor and bancassurance partner risk: Premiums collected by brokers or bank partners (an agent may not collect premium: s.38(2)) but not yet remitted to the insurer represent a credit exposure. Bank partner failures or agent insolvencies can cause premium income to be lost.

blocks.h: Operational risk is the risk of loss resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes, people, systems, or external events. For a Nigerian life insurer, the most significant operational risk categories are:

items.h: Process failure: Errors in policy administration, premium accounting, claims processing, or reinsurance accounting that result in financial loss, policyholder harm, or regulatory breach.

People risk: Key person dependency (loss of the statutory actuary, CUO, or other critical technical staff); staff fraud and misconduct; inadequate competency levels in critical roles; and high staff turnover undermining institutional knowledge.
Technology and systems risk: Policy Administration System (PAS) failures; data corruption or loss; technology obsolescence; and the failure of third-party technology providers.

Third-party and outsourcing risk: The risk that outsourced functions (IT, claims administration, agency management) are not performed to the required standard, exposing the insurer to financial loss or regulatory breach.
Legal and contract risk: Defective policy wordings, unenforceable exclusion clauses, and contractual disputes with distribution partners, reinsurers, or service providers.

blocks.h: Liquidity risk is the risk that the insurer is unable to meet its financial obligations as they fall due, without incurring unacceptable costs or disruption to its operations. Life insurance liabilities are generally longer-duration than general insurance, providing a more predictable liability profile — but several scenarios can create acute liquidity stress for a life insurer:

items.h: Mass lapse event: Economic shock or a loss of confidence in the insurer triggers a wave of simultaneous surrender requests. If the insurer’s assets are not sufficiently liquid to fund all surrenders, it may face a cash crisis.

Catastrophe claims spike: A pandemic, industrial disaster, or conflict event generating a large number of simultaneous death or disability claims in a short period. The insurer must have sufficient liquid assets to meet the claims before reinsurance recoveries are received.

Asset liquidity mismatch: An insurer that has invested heavily in illiquid assets (real estate, infrastructure, private placements) may be unable to liquidate assets quickly enough to meet unexpected claims or surrender payments without incurring significant realisation losses.

blocks.h: Regulatory risk is the risk of financial loss, reputational harm, or operational disruption arising from: changes in the regulatory environment; failure to comply with existing regulatory requirements; or adverse regulatory decisions. For Nigerian life insurers, the regulatory environment has been transformed by NIIRA 2025, and the compliance risk profile has elevated materially.

Key regulatory risk drivers under NIIRA 2025 include: RBC capital adequacy requirements and the risk of falling below the solvency threshold; mandatory claims settlement timelines and the penalties for breach; the ORSA reporting obligation; actuarial governance requirements; AML/CFT compliance; and NDPA 2023 data protection compliance. NAICOM’s expanded enforcement powers — including the ability to impose financial penalties, restrict new business writing, and replace management — mean that regulatory risk carries direct financial and operational consequences.

Reputational risk is the risk that negative public perception — arising from the insurer’s own conduct, from industry-wide events, or from external mischaracterisation — damages the brand, reduces sales, triggers policyholder lapses, or attracts regulatory scrutiny. For a life insurer in a market where public trust in the insurance sector is already fragile, reputational risk is a magnifier of all other risk categories.

In the Nigerian context, the principal reputational risk triggers for a life insurer are: claims payment failures; misleading benefit illustrations or product mis-selling; agent misconduct exposed in media; data breaches exposing customer personal or health information; and regulatory sanctions or enforcement actions. Social media has accelerated the speed at which reputational events propagate: a single viral post about a disputed claim refusal can generate thousands of negative impressions in hours, reaching audiences that advertising budgets cannot recover overnight.

Cyber risk is the risk of financial loss, operational disruption, or reputational harm arising from the failure of digital systems, from malicious cyber attacks, or from the unauthorised access to, disclosure of, or corruption of digital data. For Nigerian life insurers, the transition to digital distribution, digital underwriting, and digital claims processing — accelerated by the insurtech provisions of NIIRA 2025 — has dramatically expanded the cyber risk surface.
The principal cyber risk scenarios for a Nigerian life insurer include:

items.h: Data breach: Unauthorised access to policyholder personal data (health information, financial data, identity documents). A breach of this data is a NDPA 2023 reportable event with potential regulatory sanctions and significant reputational harm.

Ransomware attack: Malicious encryption of the insurer’s PAS, financial systems, or policy records, rendering operations impossible until a ransom is paid or systems are restored from backup. This is one of the most operationally severe cyber scenarios.

System manipulation and financial fraud: Manipulation of payment systems to redirect claim or commission payments to fraudulent accounts; false digital policy records created to support fraudulent claims.
Third-party and supply chain cyber risk: Attacks on the insurer’s technology vendors, cloud service providers, or distribution partners that create a backdoor into the insurer’s own systems.

blocks.text: 15.4.1 Defining Risk Appetite and Risk Tolerance

rows: The aggregate level and types of risk the Board is willing to accept in pursuit of the company’s strategic objectives. Risk appetite is a forward-looking, positive statement: ‘We are willing to accept X level of this risk to achieve Y strategic outcome.’

A set of qualitative risk appetite statements and quantitative limits covering each material risk category. Examples: ‘We will not accept any single-life mortality exposure in excess of ₦100m net of reinsurance’; ‘We will maintain a solvency ratio above 130% at all times’.

The acceptable degree of variation around the risk appetite level. Risk tolerance defines the boundary between acceptable and unacceptable risk outcomes. Exceeding a risk tolerance triggers a management response.
Expressed as a threshold on each KRI: the tolerance level defines when management escalates, when the Board is notified, and when regulatory reporting may be required.

Specific operational limits derived from the risk appetite, set at a granular level for individual risk drivers, business units, or products. Limits are the management tool for keeping risk within appetite.
Premium concentration limits by geography, product, or distribution channel; maximum single-life NAR net of reinsurance; minimum liquid asset ratio.

The absolute maximum risk the insurer is able to absorb before it becomes insolvent or unable to meet policyholder obligations. Risk capacity is determined by the insurer’s capital base. The Board’s risk appetite must always be set below the risk capacity.

The level of loss at which the insurer’s solvency ratio would breach the NAICOM minimum. This is the hard outer limit: risk appetite must be set sufficiently below this to provide a meaningful management buffer.

blocks.text: 15.4.2 How Boards Set and Monitor Risk Limits

blocks.h: The Board of Directors holds ultimate responsibility for risk appetite under NIIRA 2025 and the IAIS Insurance Core Principles. The Board does not manage risk operationally — that is management’s function — but the Board defines the boundaries within which management must operate. The risk appetite setting and monitoring cycle has four stages:

items.h: Setting: The Board, advised by the Chief Risk Officer (CRO) and the Board Risk Committee, agrees the risk appetite statement at the start of each strategic planning cycle. The appetite is set in the context of the company’s capital position, strategic objectives, and regulatory requirements.

Embedding: The Board-approved risk appetite is translated into specific risk limits for each business function by the CRO and senior management. Every business decision — a new product, a new distribution partnership, a significant investment — is assessed against the relevant risk limits before approval.

Monitoring: KRIs are tracked against risk limits on a monthly or quarterly basis. The CRO reports to the Board Risk Committee on any breach or near-breach of risk limits, including the root cause analysis and management response.

Review: The risk appetite statement is reviewed annually (or more frequently if the risk environment changes materially) and updated as needed. The ORSA process (Section 15.6) provides the formal analytical basis for the annual risk appetite review.

blocks.title: Risk Appetite Statement — Illustrative Extract for a Nigerian Life Insurer

blocks.h: The following is illustrative of a Board-approved risk appetite statement for a mid-sized Nigerian life insurer:

SOLVENCY: We will maintain a solvency ratio (Total Available Capital / Total Risk Charge) of no less than 140% at all times. A ratio below 140% triggers a management response plan. A ratio below 120% triggers immediate Board notification and NAICOM disclosure.

MORTALITY RISK: We will not retain net mortality exposure on any single life in excess of ₦100,000,000. We will maintain a reinsurance programme that limits our net annual mortality claims to no more than 110% of the EFU-based expected claims level in any calendar year.

LIQUIDITY: We will maintain sufficient liquid assets to fund a simultaneous 15% lapse of the in-force savings book and 150% of the expected annual death claims without selling illiquid assets. Liquid asset ratio to be reported monthly.

INVESTMENT: We will not hold more than 20% of our investment portfolio in any single asset class other than FGN bonds and Treasury bills. We will not hold more than 5% in the equity or real estate of any single issuer.

REGULATORY: We will maintain zero tolerance for wilful regulatory non-compliance. All identified regulatory breaches must be reported to the Board Audit and Risk Committee within 5 business days. A pattern of regulatory breach — more than two NAICOM compliance findings in any 12-month period — will trigger a mandatory review of the compliance function.

blocks.text: 15.5 Key Risk Indicators and the Risk Register

blocks.h: The risk register is the central document of the ERM framework — the master inventory of every risk the insurer has identified, assessed, and determined to manage. A well-maintained risk register is a living document: it is updated as new risks are identified, as the risk environment changes, and as the effectiveness of risk controls is reassessed.

rows: A unique identifier for each risk.
A clear, specific description of the risk event and its mechanism.

A sustained fall in Nigerian interest rates below 12% p.a. creates an asset-liability duration mismatch, reducing investment income below the level required to support the guaranteed benefit on the in-force savings portfolio.
The likelihood and impact of the risk before any controls are applied. Usually rated on a 5×5 matrix of likelihood × impact.
The risk management actions, systems, and processes currently in place to mitigate the risk.
Asset-liability management committee (ALCO); duration matching policy; stress-testing of investment portfolio against -5% interest rate scenario quarterly.
The likelihood and impact of the risk after applying current controls.
The executive or function responsible for managing the risk.
The metric used to monitor whether the risk is moving toward or beyond tolerance.
Portfolio modified duration gap (asset duration minus liability duration). Tolerance: ±1 year.
Any additional control or risk treatment action identified but not yet implemented.
Procure interest rate derivative instruments (interest rate swaps) to extend asset duration by Q3.

blocks.h: A Key Risk Indicator (KRI) is a quantitative metric that provides advance warning that a risk is increasing or approaching the tolerance threshold. KRIs are the monitoring instrument of the risk register: they convert abstract risk descriptions into measurable, trackable data points.

Effective KRIs share five characteristics: they are measurable (expressed as a specific number, ratio, or percentage); they are timely (available with sufficient frequency to enable a management response before the risk materialises); they are predictive (they move before the risk event, not after); they are actionable (a movement in the KRI can be linked to a specific management response); and they are owned (a named individual is responsible for monitoring and reporting each KRI).

rows: Actual-to-expected (A/E) mortality ratio on the in-force portfolio
A/E > 115%: management review. A/E > 130%: Board notification.
Year-1 lapse rate by product and distribution channel
> 20% Year-1 lapse: channel review. > 30%: product repricing assessment.
Asset-liability duration gap (asset duration minus liability duration)
Gap > 1.5 years: ALCO action plan. Gap > 2 years: Board Risk Committee escalation.
Naira equivalent value of foreign-currency assets as % of total investment portfolio
> 10%: review. > 15%: CFO approval required for any increase.
Reinsurance recoverable as % of total capital, weighted by reinsurer credit rating
Any unrated reinsurer exposure > 5% of capital: immediate review.
Claims turnaround time (average days to settlement from notification)
> 45 days average: process review. > 55 days: escalation to COO.
Number of open NAICOM regulatory findings / queries
> 3 open findings: CRO review. Any finding unresolved > 60 days: Board notification.

Any successful breach: immediate Board and NDPC notification. > 50 attempts/week: security review.
Liquid assets as % of 1-month projected cash outflows (stress scenario)
< 150%: ALCO action. < 120%: Board Risk Committee emergency meeting.

blocks.text: 15.6 The Own Risk and Solvency Assessment (ORSA)

blocks.h: A comprehensive, forward-looking internal assessment conducted by the insurer’s own management, covering: all material risks the insurer faces; the insurer’s assessment of its current and future solvency position under the RBC framework; the adequacy of its capital relative to its risk profile and strategic plan; and the key assumptions and stress scenarios used to test the robustness of the capital position. The ORSA is not a regulatory model imposed by the supervisor — it is the insurer’s own self-assessment, documented in an ORSA report submitted to the Board and to NAICOM.

The ORSA sits at the intersection of risk management and capital management. It is both a risk assessment tool (what are our risks?) and a capital planning tool (do we have enough capital to absorb them?). The ORSA is the mechanism through which the insurer’s ERM framework is formally connected to its financial management: a comprehensive risk register and KRI framework that has no connection to the capital assessment is not a complete ERM programme.

NIIRA 2025 mandates every Nigerian life insurer above a defined size threshold to conduct an annual ORSA and submit the ORSA report to NAICOM within six months of the financial year end. The mandatory contents of the ORSA report include:

items.h: A description of the insurer’s overall risk management framework, risk appetite statement, and risk governance structure.
An assessment of all material risks, including a qualitative description of each risk, the controls in place, and the residual risk rating after controls.
The insurer’s current solvency position under the NIIRA 2025 RBC framework, with a decomposition of the Total Risk Charge by component.
Forward-looking capital projections over the insurer’s strategic planning horizon (minimum 3 years), showing the projected solvency ratio under base, stress, and scenario analysis assumptions.
A description of the stress tests and scenarios used, including the rationale for their selection, the assumptions applied, and the results of each scenario.
The insurer’s assessment of its own capital needs — the level of capital it considers appropriate given its specific risk profile — which may differ from the regulatory minimum.
The actions the Board and management would take if the solvency ratio fell below defined trigger levels, including capital raising options, reinsurance adjustments, and business plan modifications.

blocks.h: NAICOM may use the ORSA report as the basis for supervisory dialogue: if NAICOM’s review of the ORSA identifies risks or vulnerabilities not adequately addressed by the insurer, NAICOM may impose additional capital requirements or operational restrictions. The ORSA therefore serves both an internal management function and a regulatory transparency function.

blocks.text: 15.6.3 Conducting the ORSA: A Process Framework

items.h: Define scope and materiality thresholds: Identify all risk categories to be included and set the materiality threshold below which risks are noted but not stress-tested in depth.
Update the risk register: Review and update all risk entries, residual risk ratings, and KRI status. Identify any new risks that have emerged since the last ORSA.

Run the base case capital projection: Project the insurer’s solvency ratio over the planning horizon using the base case business plan assumptions. This provides the starting point against which stress scenarios are applied.

Design stress tests and scenarios: Select a range of stress scenarios that test the most material individual risk drivers (a mortality shock, an interest rate crash, a mass lapse event) and combined scenarios (economic recession triggering simultaneously: higher lapses, lower investment returns, and deteriorating credit quality).

Run stress test models: The actuarial function runs the capital model under each stress scenario and records the solvency ratio impact. The reverse stress test — identifying the scenario under which the insurer’s solvency ratio would breach the regulatory minimum — is a required ORSA component.

Assess capital adequacy and management actions: Evaluate whether the capital position is sufficient under all scenarios, and document the management actions available to restore solvency if any scenario breaches the tolerance.

Board review and approval: The ORSA report is presented to the Board for review and formal approval. The Board must engage with the findings, challenge assumptions, and record its conclusions in the Board minutes.
NAICOM submission: The approved ORSA report is submitted to NAICOM within the prescribed timeline.

blocks.text: 15.7 Risk Governance: CRO, Board Risk Committee, and Three Lines of Defence

blocks.h: The Chief Risk Officer (CRO) is the executive responsible for the design, implementation, and ongoing operation of the insurer’s ERM framework. NIIRA 2025 requires life insurers above defined thresholds to appoint a CRO, who must meet NAICOM’s fit and proper requirements. The CRO’s principal responsibilities are:

items.h: Owning the ERM framework: maintaining the risk management policy, risk register, and KRI framework; ensuring they are embedded in business operations.

Independent risk oversight: providing the Board and senior management with an independent assessment of the risk profile — independent from the business functions that take on risk. The CRO must be able to challenge business proposals on risk grounds without commercial pressure overriding the risk assessment.
ORSA leadership: coordinating and owning the annual ORSA process, working with the Statutory Actuary on the capital modelling components.
Risk reporting: producing monthly and quarterly risk reports for senior management and the Board Risk Committee, including KRI dashboards, risk register updates, and emerging risk monitoring.
Regulatory engagement: serving as the primary interface with NAICOM on risk management matters; coordinating the ORSA submission; responding to NAICOM risk-related supervisory queries.

blocks.h: The CRO should report to the CEO operationally but have a direct reporting line to the Board Risk Committee on matters where independence from management is required — particularly the ORSA findings and any disagreements with management on risk-taking decisions. The effectiveness of the CRO function depends critically on this independence.

The Board Risk Committee (BRC) is the Board-level governance body responsible for overseeing the ERM framework on behalf of the full Board. Under NIIRA 2025, life insurers are required to have a Board Risk Committee (which may be combined with the Audit Committee as a Board Audit and Risk Committee in smaller organisations) with defined terms of reference.

The BRC’s mandate includes: reviewing and approving the risk appetite statement; receiving and reviewing the quarterly risk management report from the CRO; approving the ORSA report before NAICOM submission; reviewing significant risk limit breaches and management’s responses; overseeing the independence and effectiveness of the risk function; and providing input into the Board’s overall risk culture.

BRC members must include at least one independent Non-Executive Director with financial risk management experience. The Statutory Actuary should present to the BRC at least annually on the actuarial risk components of the ORSA and valuation results. The external auditor should have access to the BRC for reporting on risk-related audit findings.

blocks.text: 15.7.3 The Three Lines of Defence Model

blocks.title: The Three Lines of Defence Model in Life Insurance

blocks.h: The Three Lines of Defence (3LoD) model is the internationally recognised framework for assigning risk management responsibilities across the organisation. It defines three distinct roles, with clear accountability and independence from each other:

FIRST LINE — Business Functions (Own and Manage Risk). The first line comprises all operational functions that take on risk in the course of business: sales and distribution, underwriting, claims, investment management, product development, IT operations. The first line is responsible for identifying and managing the risks in their own activities, within the risk limits set by the Board. Risk ownership and control are embedded in the first line’s day-to-day processes, not delegated to a separate risk function.

SECOND LINE — Risk and Compliance Functions (Oversee and Challenge). The second line comprises the CRO and the risk management function, the compliance function, and the actuarial function. The second line provides independent oversight of the first line’s risk-taking: it sets risk policies and frameworks; monitors KRIs and escalates breaches; conducts the ORSA; and challenges first-line business decisions that approach or breach risk limits. Crucially, the second line does not own the underlying business risks — it oversees them.

THIRD LINE — Internal Audit (Independent Assurance). The third line is the internal audit function, which provides independent assurance to the Board and Audit Committee that the first and second lines are operating effectively. Internal audit does not own or manage risks — it assesses whether the systems of control and oversight in the first and second lines are fit for purpose. Internal audit’s independence from the first and second lines is essential: the Chief Internal Auditor should report directly to the Board Audit Committee, not to the CEO or CRO.

blocks.title: Common 3LoD Failures in Nigerian Life Insurance Practice

blocks.h: The following governance failures undermine the 3LoD model and are commonly observed in the Nigerian market:

items.h: The CRO reports only to the CEO, with no direct line to the Board Risk Committee — eliminating the independence that makes the second line effective.
The risk function is combined with the compliance function and staffed at a junior level, leaving the CRO with insufficient seniority or authority to challenge business decisions.
Internal audit reports to the CFO or CEO rather than to the Board Audit Committee, compromising its independence from the management it is auditing.
The Board Risk Committee meets infrequently (quarterly or less) and does not engage substantively with risk reports — treating the BRC as a formality rather than a governance mechanism.

The first line delegates all risk management activity to the CRO, creating the false impression that risk is ‘managed’ by a central function while business units bear no responsibility for their own risk-taking.

blocks.h: Catastrophe risks are low-frequency, high-severity events that can generate a large number of simultaneous insurance claims, overwhelming the insurer’s normal claims experience and potentially breaching reinsurance programme limits. Three catastrophe risk categories are particularly material for Nigerian life insurers:

The COVID-19 pandemic of 2020–22 was the most significant mortality shock to global life insurance portfolios in a generation. In Nigeria, the direct mortality impact of COVID-19 was lower than in high-income countries (due to demographic factors — Nigeria’s relatively young population — and possible underreporting), but the indirect effects were significant: economic contraction increased lapse rates; healthcare system disruption reduced access to medical evidence for underwriting; and the operational disruption of lockdowns stressed insurers’ paper-dependent processes.

For life insurers, pandemic risk is assessed through pandemic stress tests: the actuary models the impact of an elevated mortality scenario — typically expressing a percentage increase in the qx values across all ages over a defined period — on the portfolio’s claims cost and reserve adequacy. NIIRA 2025’s ORSA requirement mandates that pandemic risk be included as a named stress scenario in the annual ORSA.

Risk management responses to pandemic risk include: mortality catastrophe reinsurance covers with pandemic triggers; geographic diversification of the in-force portfolio to limit concentration in single high-risk areas; and operational BCM planning for business continuity during a public health emergency.

Nigeria experiences significant annual flooding, particularly in the Niger Delta region, the Middle Belt flood plains (Benue, Kogi, Anambra states), and coastal zones. The 2022 Nigeria floods, among the worst in decades, resulted in over 600 deaths, displaced millions of people, and caused billions of Naira in economic losses. Life insurance portfolios with significant exposure to vulnerable geographic zones face elevated mortality and morbidity risk from flooding.

From a life insurance perspective, flood risk operates through several channels: direct mortality from drowning and flood-related injuries; post-flood mortality from waterborne disease outbreaks (cholera, typhoid); displacement disrupting healthcare access for chronic disease patients; and the economic disruption of agricultural communities reducing premium affordability and driving policy lapses.

Geographic risk concentration monitoring — tracking the aggregate sum assured exposed in flood-vulnerable zones — is a necessary component of the ERM framework for Nigerian life insurers. Portfolio rebalancing, geographic premium loading, and flood catastrophe reinsurance are the primary risk management tools.

Parts of northern Nigeria, the Middle Belt, and the South South region have experienced elevated mortality from armed conflict, banditry, and civil unrest over extended periods. The life insurance implications are direct: policyholders in high-risk security zones have elevated mortality risk; group life schemes covering employees of organisations operating in conflict-affected areas (military contractors, telecoms companies, NGOs) face elevated claims; and the operational capacity of the insurer’s own branches and distribution networks in affected areas may be compromised.

Most Nigerian life insurance policies include a war and civil commotion exclusion that limits the insurer’s liability for deaths directly attributable to war or military action. However, the precise boundaries of these exclusions in the context of the Nigerian security environment — banditry, farmer-herder conflict, kidnapping-related deaths — are not always clear, creating claims assessment complexity and potential for disputes. The ERM framework must address: the geographic concentration of the in-force portfolio in high-risk security zones; the adequacy and legal precision of policy exclusions; and the operational security of staff and agents.

NIIRA 2025 requires every licensed life insurer to establish, implement, and maintain a written Risk Management Framework (RMF) that meets NAICOM’s prescribed minimum standards. The mandatory components of the RMF under NIIRA 2025 are:

items.h: A Board-approved risk management policy, stating the insurer’s risk philosophy, risk appetite, risk governance structure, and the roles and responsibilities of all risk management functions.
A risk identification and assessment process, including the maintenance of a risk register updated at least quarterly.
A KRI monitoring and reporting framework, with defined escalation procedures for tolerance breaches.
A stress testing programme covering all material risk categories and scenarios, conducted at least annually.
An internal capital assessment process aligned with the RBC framework, including the annual ORSA.
A BCM plan covering all critical business processes, with annual testing and Board approval.
Policies covering specific risk areas: investment risk policy; reinsurance risk policy; operational risk policy; cyber security policy; AML/CFT policy; and data protection policy.

blocks.text: 15.9.2 NAICOM Supervisory Powers in Respect of Risk Management

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025 gives NAICOM extensive supervisory powers in the risk management domain. These include:

items.h: RMF inspection: NAICOM may inspect the insurer’s ERM documentation, risk register, KRI reports, ORSA, and Board risk committee minutes as part of its annual supervisory review or a targeted thematic inspection.

Capital add-on: Where NAICOM’s review of the ORSA or the RBC calculation identifies risks that the insurer’s own model does not adequately capture, NAICOM may impose a capital add-on — requiring the insurer to hold additional capital above the standard RBC minimum.

Business restriction: Where NAICOM identifies material risk management deficiencies, it may restrict the insurer from writing new business in specified product lines or distribution channels until the deficiencies are remediated.
Management intervention: In cases of serious risk management failure, NAICOM may direct the replacement of the CRO, Statutory Actuary, or other key risk management personnel.

Enforceable undertakings: NAICOM may require the insurer to enter into a formal written undertaking to implement specified risk management improvements within defined timelines, with financial penalties for non-compliance.

blocks.text: 15.10 Business Continuity Management and Disaster Recovery

blocks.h: Business Continuity Management (BCM) is the process of ensuring that critical business operations can continue, or be rapidly restored, in the event of a major disruption. For a life insurance company, the business processes that must continue even in a major disruption include: premium collection and policy administration; claims notification and payment; customer service for policyholders; reinsurance accounting; and the regulatory reporting cycle.
A BCM framework aligned with ISO 22301 (Business Continuity Management Systems) comprises the following components:

rows: An assessment of the impact of disruption to each critical business process, including the maximum tolerable period of disruption (MTPD) before the disruption causes irreversible harm, and the minimum business continuity objective (MBCO) — the minimum level of service that must be maintained.

Documented recovery procedures for each critical process, specifying: the trigger for activating the plan; the recovery team and their contact details; the step-by-step recovery actions; the alternative locations, systems, and resources required; and the communication protocol for staff, customers, and regulators.

The technical component of BCM: the backup and recovery systems that enable the insurer to restore its IT infrastructure — the PAS, financial systems, and communication tools — within the Recovery Time Objective (RTO) set in the BIA.

The overarching plan activated when a disruptive event occurs, governing: the activation of BCPs; the crisis communications strategy (for staff, customers, reinsurers, NAICOM, and the media); and the escalation path to Board level.

BCPs must be tested at least annually through tabletop exercises, live drills, or simulated disasters. Test results must be documented and used to update the plans. NIIRA 2025 requires the BCM plan to be reviewed and Board-approved at least annually.

blocks.text: 15.10.2 BCM in the Nigerian Operating Environment

blocks.h: Nigerian life insurers face specific BCM challenges beyond those encountered in more stable markets. Power supply unreliability is a pervasive operational risk: extended grid failures can disable branch operations, IT systems, and customer service centres. Generator dependency creates a secondary risk from fuel supply disruptions. BCM plans must address power continuity explicitly, including battery backup systems, generator maintenance protocols, and cloud-based system hosting that reduces local power dependency.

Physical security threats — robbery, civil unrest, and in some regions security incidents — may require branch evacuations and temporary closure of operational locations. BCM plans for branch-dependent insurers must specify the alternative service delivery channels (digital, telephone, neighbouring branch) that can be activated when a branch is inaccessible.

The shift to cloud-based PAS and digital distribution reduces some BCM risks (system redundancy, geographic backup) while introducing new ones (vendor dependency, data sovereignty concerns under NDPA 2023, and the cyber risks associated with cloud access). BCM and IT DR plans must address the specific architecture of the insurer’s technology infrastructure, not rely on generic templates.

blocks.text: 15.11 Climate Risk Assessment for Nigerian Life Insurers

blocks.h: Climate risk for financial institutions is conventionally categorised into two dimensions, as defined by the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD), whose framework is increasingly referenced in insurance regulation globally and is reflected in NAICOM’s emerging climate risk supervisory posture.

rows: Risk from discrete weather events of increasing severity or frequency: floods, storms, droughts, extreme heat events.

Elevated mortality and morbidity from flood events (Niger Delta, Benue valley, coastal cities); heat-related illness mortality in northern states; vector-borne disease range expansion (malaria, dengue) linked to temperature rise; displacement-driven lapses in climate-vulnerable communities.
Risk from long-term shifts in climate patterns: rising average temperatures, changing precipitation patterns, sea level rise.

Long-term deterioration in population health outcomes in chronically affected regions, affecting the EFU mortality basis; food insecurity-linked health deterioration in agricultural communities; coastal zone settlement risk affecting the geographic distribution of the insured population.
Risk from changes in government policy in response to climate change: carbon pricing, energy transition regulations, fossil fuel restrictions.

Investment portfolio risk: companies in carbon-intensive sectors (oil and gas, petrochemicals) may face stranded asset risk as Nigeria transitions toward its Paris Agreement commitments. Life insurers with significant oil and gas equity holdings face capital value risk.
Risk from the disruption caused by new climate-aligned technologies: clean energy, electric vehicles, green infrastructure.

Investment portfolio reorientation risk: a rapid transition to renewable energy creates both investment opportunity (green bonds, renewable energy infrastructure) and transition risk (fossil fuel asset write-downs).

blocks.text: 15.11.2 Incorporating Climate Risk into the ERM Framework

blocks.h: Climate risk is not yet a standard item in most Nigerian life insurers’ risk registers. NAICOM has begun issuing supervisory guidance on climate risk disclosure expectations, aligned with international frameworks including the TCFD and the NGFS (Network for Greening the Financial System). The trajectory is clear: climate risk will become a formal ERM and ORSA requirement for Nigerian insurers within the medium-term regulatory horizon.
Practical steps Nigerian life insurers should take to incorporate climate risk into their ERM framework in the near term include:

items.h: Portfolio geographic analysis: Map the in-force policy portfolio against Nigeria’s flood risk zones (using NIHSA — Nigerian Hydrological Services Agency — maps) to identify concentration risk in high-vulnerability areas.
Investment portfolio carbon exposure: Assess the proportion of the investment portfolio in carbon-intensive sectors and model the impact of a carbon pricing scenario on asset values.

Mortality assumption stress: Include a long-term climate mortality stress in the ORSA — a scenario in which the EFU qx values for the population in the most climate-vulnerable geographic zones are increased by a defined percentage over a 10-year horizon.
TCFD disclosure readiness: Prepare for TCFD-aligned climate risk disclosure requirements that NAICOM and the SEC are expected to formalise for listed insurers within the medium term.

blocks.text: 15.12 Advisory: Building an ERM Function in a Nigerian Life Insurance Company

blocks.h: The gap between having an ERM policy document (a compliance artefact) and having a genuinely functioning ERM culture (a strategic capability) is the most significant risk management challenge facing most Nigerian life insurers. This advisory section addresses the practical steps for building ERM from the ground up, or materially strengthening an existing framework.

blocks.title: Advisory: A Four-Phase ERM Maturity Journey for Nigerian Life Insurers

blocks.h: Most Nigerian life insurers currently sit between Phase 1 and Phase 2 of the following maturity model. The transition to Phase 3 and 4 is the regulatory and commercial expectation under NIIRA 2025:

PHASE 1 — COMPLIANCE-DRIVEN (Reactive): ERM exists primarily as a compliance obligation. A risk policy document is maintained for NAICOM purposes. Risk reporting is produced periodically but not actively used in management decisions. No CRO; risk function is part-time or combined with compliance. Risk register exists but is rarely updated.

PHASE 2 — STRUCTURED (Systematic): A dedicated CRO is appointed. The risk register is actively maintained with quarterly updates. KRIs are defined and tracked monthly. The ORSA is conducted annually and submitted to NAICOM. The Board Risk Committee meets quarterly. Risk reports are used by the ExCo in decision-making.

PHASE 3 — INTEGRATED (Proactive): Risk appetite is fully integrated with the strategic plan and business performance management. Every material business decision is accompanied by a risk assessment against appetite limits. The 3LoD model is genuinely implemented. Stress testing is used to inform capital allocation and product pricing. Climate and cyber risks are formally assessed in the ORSA.

PHASE 4 — EMBEDDED (Cultural): Risk management is part of the company’s DNA. Every employee understands their risk management responsibility. Risk culture is measured and reported to the Board. ERM creates genuine competitive advantage: better pricing accuracy, faster response to opportunities, lower cost of capital from a demonstrably strong risk governance posture. NAICOM views the insurer as a risk management exemplar.

blocks.title: The Single Most Important ERM Investment for a Nigerian Life Insurer

blocks.h: When resources are constrained and an insurer must prioritise its ERM investment, data quality and the risk register come before all else. An insurer that does not have reliable, complete, timely data on its own portfolio — its in-force policies by age, geography, and product type; its actual mortality and lapse experience; its reinsurance recoveries; its expense per policy — cannot assess its own risks meaningfully. The most sophisticated ERM framework built on unreliable data produces confident answers to the wrong questions.

Practical priority: Before hiring a CRO or building a KRI dashboard, invest in data governance: a single source of truth for the policy portfolio; automated monthly experience reporting (actual vs. expected mortality, lapse rates, expense ratios); and a PAS that produces actuarially reliable output. The risk register built on clean data, regularly updated, and reviewed by the Board is worth more than an elaborate ERM infrastructure built on data the insurer cannot trust.
The systematic, organisation-wide process of identifying, assessing, and managing all risks faced by an insurer, integrated with strategy and capital management, and subject to Board governance.

The international standard for risk management principles, framework, and process, published by the International Organization for Standardization. Provides the universal language and process architecture for ERM across all sectors.

The Enterprise Risk Management framework published by the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission. Explicitly integrates risk management with strategic planning and performance management.

The global supervisory standards for insurance regulation published by the International Association of Insurance Supervisors. ICP 8 and ICP 16 set the ERM and ORSA expectations that NAICOM’s NIIRA 2025 requirements reflect.

The risk that actual policyholder mortality, morbidity, longevity, or lapse experience differs adversely from the assumptions used in pricing and reserving. The primary risk category for a life insurer.
The risk of financial loss from adverse movements in financial market prices, including interest rates, equity values, real estate prices, exchange rates, and inflation.
The risk of loss from the default or credit quality deterioration of a counterparty, including bond issuers in the investment portfolio, reinsurers, and distribution partners.
The risk of loss from inadequate or failed internal processes, people, systems, or external events, including process errors, staff fraud, IT system failures, and third-party failures.
The risk that the insurer cannot meet its financial obligations as they fall due without incurring unacceptable costs, triggered by mass lapses, catastrophe claims, or asset-liability mismatch.
The aggregate level and types of risk the Board is willing to accept in the pursuit of the company’s strategic objectives.
The acceptable degree of variation around the risk appetite level; the boundary between outcomes that trigger management action and those that do not.
The central document of the ERM framework, cataloguing all identified material risks with their descriptions, inherent and residual risk ratings, controls, owners, and KRIs.
A quantitative metric that provides advance warning that a risk is increasing toward or beyond the tolerance threshold. Effective KRIs are measurable, timely, predictive, actionable, and owned.

A comprehensive forward-looking internal assessment of the insurer’s material risks and its current and projected solvency position under base and stress scenarios. Mandatory under NIIRA 2025; submitted annually to NAICOM.

A risk governance model assigning risk management responsibilities to: the first line (business functions that own and manage risks); the second line (CRO and risk/compliance functions that oversee and challenge); and the third line (internal audit that provides independent assurance).
The executive responsible for the ERM framework, risk monitoring, ORSA, and independent risk oversight. Required for Nigerian life insurers above defined thresholds under NIIRA 2025.
A stress test that identifies the scenario under which the insurer’s solvency ratio would breach the regulatory minimum. Required as part of the ORSA under NIIRA 2025.
The process of ensuring critical business operations can continue or be rapidly restored following a major disruption, governed by a Board-approved BCM plan tested at least annually.
The component of BCM that assesses the impact of disruption to each critical business process, including the Maximum Tolerable Period of Disruption and the Minimum Business Continuity Objective.
The risk of financial loss arising from the physical impacts of climate change, including acute events (floods, storms) and chronic shifts (rising temperatures, changing precipitation).

The risk of financial loss arising from the economic and policy adjustments required to transition to a lower-carbon economy, including carbon pricing, stranded fossil fuel assets, and technological disruption.

Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures: an international framework for reporting climate-related risks and opportunities, whose recommendations are increasingly reflected in financial sector regulation.
